params.name: dem_rate
params.label: Demographic (population + aging) growth of radiologist work, 2026-2045
params.note: Christensen et al project +16.9% to +26.9% exams by modality 2023-2055 from population growth and aging alone (≈0.49-0.75%/yr) using Census 2023 projections. CBO's 2026 outlook has slower population growth (349M→364M, 2026-2056), so the centre is shaded down ≈0.1 pt.

params.name: dem_late
params.label: Demographic growth in 2066 relative to 2026-2045 rate
params.note: CBO projects population growth slowing to zero by 2056; aging continues to add imaging per capita.

params.name: util_g0
params.label: Per-capita (age/sex-adjusted) utilization growth, 2026
params.note: National 2018-22 claims (Christensen et al): projected total utilization in 2055 vs 2023 is +16.9% to +26.9% by modality from population growth and aging alone, and -5.6% to +45.2% if each modality's recent per-person trend continues to 2030 (radiography and nuclear medicine falling, CT and MRI rising). The Neiman Institute's 2026 update projects +17% (MRI) to +25% (CT) by 2055. Older health-system data show faster CT growth (3.7-5.2%/yr, 2013-16) and ED CT per Medicare beneficiary nearly doubled 2013-2023. Each end of the trend range is a single modality (CT up, nuclear medicine down), so a work-weighted claims-based figure is lower than CT's. Version 1.5 centred per-person growth at 0.6%/yr (σ 0.7). The history test (model/history.py) needs radiologist work per person to have grown about 2.2%/yr in 2022-2026 (80%: 1.1-2.9; about 1.8%/yr after removing complexity growth) to explain today's shortage, but that estimate is barely narrower than the range it started from, shares sources with the claims-based view, and is about 0.5 points lower without the market adjustment. The centre, 1.2%/yr, halfway between, is therefore a judgment informed by both. The spread is 1.5 times v1.5's, a width that tied with 1.0 on the fitting episodes and did better on the held-out ones (wider still did better there, but choosing on held-out years would leak). Growth decays toward ~0.2%/yr. The 'imaging restraint' prior set (near claims-based trends) and 'imaging growth' (the history estimate) bracket it.

params.name: util_ginf
params.label: Long-run per-capita utilization growth (asymptote)
params.note: Growth in CT/MRI per capita has decelerated each decade since 2000; we assume further deceleration but allow either sign. Spread 1.5 times v1.5's, as for the current rate.

params.name: util_half
params.label: Half-life of convergence from current to long-run utilization growth

params.name: cmplx_g0
params.label: Growth in radiologist work per exam (complexity, images/study), 2026
params.note: Images per cross-sectional study rose ~10x at Mayo 1999-2010 while exams doubled. Work per exam (RVU-weighted) grows far more slowly than image counts; we decay this term with a 20-year half-life.

params.name: alt_max
params.label: Imaging displaced by alternative diagnostics by 2066 (blood tests, AI-ECG, genomics)

params.name: alt_mid
params.label: Midpoint year of alternative-diagnostic substitution

params.name: ratio0
params.label: Supply ÷ demand for radiologist FTEs in 2026 (current shortage)
params.note: No measured national figure exists; this is a judgment from indirect signals. HRSA projects radiology at ≈90% adequacy in 2038 (a projection, not today's gap), and the Neiman Institute calls the shortage 'fairly static'. Compensation rose 6.6% in a year and DR positions keep expanding. Average exams read per radiologist-day were flat 2018-2024 (+0.6%) but the busiest quartile read 31% more, and practice turnover rose from 5.3% to 8.5% (2013-2022): a real but uneven, moderate shortage. The history reconstruction (model/history.py), which fits the documented job market since 1995, puts 2026 at 0.95 (80%: 0.92-0.98) with the market adjustment and 0.88 without it, and its 2022-2025 episode was coded from some of the same signals. v1.5's judgment was Triangular(0.85, 0.93, 0.99); this prior is one judgment informed by that model-dependent reconstruction, not an independent second estimate.

params.name: ai_u
params.label: AI progress speed (quantile → timeline multiplier M)
params.dist: Regime mixture: 15% stall (M 1.6-3.0), 55% trend (lognormal, median 1, σ_log 0.25), 18% fast (M 0.40-0.65), 12% transformative (M 0.25-0.45, task ceilings lifted)
params.note: Loose guidance only; M multiplies the years from 2026 until each capability arrives. AI researchers put 50% odds on machines outperforming humans at every task by 2047 but on full automation of occupations only by 2116; expert panels put far lower odds on near-term transformative AI than lab leaders. Fast + transformative = 30% of worlds.

params.name: cap_draft_T0
params.label: Midpoint year: reliable draft reports & automated measurements (M=1)
params.note: Generative draft reporting gave +15.5% documentation efficiency on 24k radiographs in live use; AI-drafted chest radiograph reports cut reading time 42% in a reader study; generative chest-radiograph drafting tools received FDA Breakthrough designations in 2026.

params.name: cap_admin_T0
params.label: Midpoint year: protocoling, scheduling, QA and admin automation (M=1)

params.name: cap_interp_T0
params.label: Midpoint year: AI assistance that materially speeds interpretation (M=1)
params.note: Real-world meta-analysis finds no significant time savings yet; effects of AI assistance vary widely across radiologists and erroneous AI output hurts performance; radiologists under-weight AI predictions.

params.name: cap_consult_T0
params.label: Midpoint year: AI support for clinical synthesis/communication (M=1)

params.name: cap_proc_T0
params.label: Midpoint year: meaningful automation of procedural/physical work (M=1)

params.name: cap_width
params.label: Capability S-curve width (logistic scale; 10→90% ≈ 4.4×)

params.name: m_interp
params.label: Max time saved on interpretation by assistive AI (radiologist still reads)
params.note: Langlotz's task analysis and reader studies of AI assistance. (European screening workload cuts of 33-44% come from replacing the second reader in double reading, a substitution effect that does not transfer to single-read U.S. practice, so they are not used here.)

params.name: m_draft
params.label: Max time saved on measurement & report drafting
params.note: Measured savings span 0% to 42% of reading time: +15.5% (live radiographs), −42% (chest-radiograph reader study), −0.46 min per impression (multicentre LLM study), and no sustained gain at one of two CT sites. If drafting and measurement are ~30% of reading time, current tools already capture roughly half of this sub-task.

params.name: m_consult
params.label: Max time saved on clinical synthesis/consultation/communication
params.note: Langlotz: record summarization −30% tech/provider communication; non-routine communication −30%; patient explanation −30%.

params.name: m_admin
params.label: Max time saved on administrative work (protocoling, QA, scheduling)
params.note: Langlotz: automated protocoling −60% (30-70%).

params.name: m_proc
params.label: Max time saved on physical/procedural work

params.name: adopt_mid
params.label: Midpoint year of effective clinical adoption of assistive AI
params.note: ≈1,100 radiology AI devices cleared by 2025 but claims-based use was concentrated in a handful of products; 33.5% of US radiologists reported using any AI in 2020, and 75% of UK departments used AI clinically in 2025 without an overall workload reduction. Precedent: mammography CAD reached most US screening exams within ~6 years of payment.

params.name: adopt_pressure
params.label: Shortage acceleration of AI adoption (extra adoption-clock speed per unit ln(D/S))
params.note: Practices adopt labour-saving AI faster when radiologists are scarce. At a 7% shortage and the midpoint value (2), assistive and autonomous adoption clocks run ~14% faster. Applied only while demand exceeds supply.

params.name: adopt_width
params.label: Assistive adoption S-curve width

params.name: adopt_max
params.label: Saturation share of work done with assistive AI

params.name: ovh_max
params.label: New oversight work created by AI (governance, auditing, validation), share of time
params.note: Langlotz does not model AI monitoring/oversight time. In Danish administrative data, chatbot adoption created new integration and oversight tasks that offset most of a ~3% time saving.

params.name: w1
params.label: Tier 1 share of interpretive work: normal/negative radiographs & screening exams
params.note: AI could autonomously report 7.8% of all posteroanterior chest radiographs at >99% sensitivity (2023) and ~17.5% at 99% sensitivity with a tuned threshold (2024); AI triage let about two-thirds of Danish screening mammograms be single-read (33.5% fewer reads), though that saving comes from European double reading and U.S. screening is single-read. Radiographs and screening mammography are ~20-25% of radiologist work, so tier 1 is ≈4-12% of interpretive work.

params.name: w2
params.label: Tier 2 share: all radiographs, screening mammography, standardized follow-ups
params.note: Langlotz delegation assumptions: mammography 50%, radiography 40%, other modalities 3%.

params.name: w3
params.label: Tier 3 share: complex diagnostic CT/MR/US/NM

params.name: tcap1_T0
params.label: Tier 1 technical capability year (not AI-speed scaled)
params.note: An autonomous normal-chest-radiograph product received EU CE Class IIb marking in 2022.

params.name: tcap2_T0
params.label: Tier 2 technical capability year (M=1)

params.name: tcap3_T0
params.label: Tier 3 technical capability year (M=1)

params.name: tcap4_T0
params.label: Tier 4 (residual hardest work) capability year (M=1)

params.name: lval
params.label: Clinical-validation lag (prospective, multi-site) after capability; tier-1 median
params.note: MASAI randomised from April 2021; its interval-cancer endpoint was published in January 2026 (~5 years). 43% of FDA-authorised AI devices had no published clinical validation and only 4% had randomised trials. Tiers 2-4 multiply by 1.2/1.5/1.8.

params.name: lfda
params.label: FDA authorization lag for autonomous claims; tier-2 median
params.note: As of October 2026 no autonomous radiology read is FDA-authorized; generative report drafting has reached FDA Breakthrough designation (2026) and one 510(k) report-generating tool keeps the radiologist in control; FDA's AI lifecycle guidance remains a draft. IDx-DR (2018) is the main autonomous precedent. Tier multipliers 0.75/1.0/1.5/2.0.

params.name: lpay
params.label: Liability + reimbursement + scope-of-practice acceptance lag; tier-2 median
params.note: Autonomous retinal AI: FDA 2018 → Category I CPT 92229 in 2021. Mock jurors penalize radiologists who disagree with AI. Medicare professional-component billing presumes physician interpretation. Tier multipliers 0.75/1.0/1.4/1.8.

params.name: ahalf
params.label: Hospital adoption: years from 'ready' to half of eventual uptake
params.note: Hospital EHR adoption passed 50% about four years after the 2009 HITECH subsidies; reimbursed mammography CAD diffused within ≈4-6 years.

params.name: awidth
params.label: Autonomy adoption S-curve width

params.name: amax1
params.label: Eventual uptake of tier-1 autonomy (share of eligible work)

params.name: amax2
params.label: Eventual uptake of tier-2 autonomy

params.name: amax3
params.label: Eventual uptake of tier-3 autonomy

params.name: amax4
params.label: Eventual uptake of tier-4 autonomy

params.name: f_sub
params.label: Share of interpretation+drafting time actually removed per AI-first/autonomous study
params.note: Residual human time: sampling QA, sign-off, escalations, liability review. Clinically significant errors still appeared in 22.8% of AI-only versus 14.0% of human-only chest-radiograph reports in a 2025 evaluation.

params.name: pc_share
params.label: Professional (interpretation) share of the all-in price of an imaging exam
params.note: ≈20% for MRI, ≈25% for radiography of Medicare global fees; lower where hospital facility fees apply.

params.name: pass_through
params.label: Share of cost savings passed through to prices paid
params.note: Fee schedules are administered and revalued slowly; commercial prices are sticky.

params.name: elasticity
params.label: Price elasticity of imaging demand
params.note: RAND HIE ≈ −0.2 for medical care, with respect to the patient's out-of-pocket price; professional-fee cuts mostly fall on payers, so this channel is if anything overstated. Deductible shocks cut imaging alongside other services.

params.name: access
params.label: Turnaround/availability rebound: extra work per unit of radiologist time freed
params.note: Non-price rationing: when reads become fast and available 24/7, clinicians order more (ED CT visits rose from 2.8% to 13.9%, 1995-2007). Applied to the share of radiologist time saved.

params.name: new_max
params.label: New AI-enabled imaging applications by 2066 (share of baseline work, before capacity limits)
params.note: Of 2024 imaging studies with direct patient-care impact, 49% would increase radiologist workload and <1% would decrease it; AI studies were about 14 times higher odds of adding work (odds ratio 14.3). Examples: opportunistic CT screening, lung screening (18% uptake in 2022), AI coronary plaque analysis (Category I CPT 75577 from 2026).

params.name: new_T0
params.label: Midpoint year of new-application uptake (M=1)

params.name: new_width
params.label: New-application S-curve width

params.name: lambda_new
params.label: Radiologist labour intensity of new-application work vs a typical exam

params.name: iota
params.label: Extra follow-up work from AI-detected (incidental) findings at full deployment
params.note: AI-supported screening raised cancer detection 17.6-29% with flat recall; more findings mean more follow-up.

params.name: latent
params.label: Latent demand currently rationed by scanner/technologist capacity
params.note: CT technologist vacancy 19.4% and MRI 17.4% in 2025.

params.name: thru_H
params.label: AI-driven acquisition throughput gain at maturity (faster scans, auto-positioning)
params.note: Deep-learning reconstruction cut knee MRI time ≈44% prospectively; CT is already fast and table time dominates.

params.name: thru_T0
params.label: Midpoint year of throughput gains (M=1)

params.name: cap_invest
params.label: Long-run extra scanner/technologist capacity built in response to demand (by 2066)

params.name: um_max
params.label: AI-enabled utilization management (order decision support, payer AI prior auth)
params.note: Langlotz: order-entry decision support −3% (0-6%) of advanced imaging; Medicare HI trust fund depletion projected 2033.

params.name: scope_max
params.label: Reads shifting to non-radiologists with AI support by 2066

params.name: nt_max
params.label: New radiologist tasks created alongside AI (reinstatement), share of 2026 FTE
params.note: e.g. AI governance roles, theranostics, quantitative-imaging consults, multidisciplinary precision-medicine work.

params.name: attr_mult
params.label: Attrition hazard multiplier (post-COVID ≈ high end)
params.note: Measured attrition rose from 1.1%/yr (2014) to 2.0% (2019) and 2.5% (2022). With flat residency positions, multipliers of 1.0 and 1.2 reproduce the published supply projections under blended 2014-23 attrition (+25.7% by 2055) and post-COVID attrition (+20.9%); the range is centred between them, nearer the post-COVID case the Neiman 2026 update emphasises. Turnover between practices also roughly doubled (adjusted odds 1.96, 2022 vs 2013).

params.name: slot_g
params.label: Trend growth in DR residency positions (before market response)
params.note: DR positions rose 33% from 2010 to 2025 (about 1.9%/yr) and from 1,132 (2022) to 1,241 (2026), about 2.3%/yr. We centre slightly lower (1.5%/yr) because Medicare GME caps bind and PGY-1 applicants fell 14% over 2023-2026; the 'residency growth continues' prior set uses 1.9%/yr.

params.name: resid_gamma
params.label: Residency-position response to market signal (elasticity to ln D/S)
params.note: After the mid-1990s downturn, radiology trainee numbers fell to a 1997 nadir (3,080) and then rose 84% by 2011; medical-student interest tracks the job market.

params.name: fill_kappa
params.label: Fill-rate response to oversupply (applicant flight)
params.note: 2015 Match, during the last oversupply: 86% of advanced DR positions filled, 55 of 166 programs went unfilled, and U.S. graduates took 67% of matched positions.

params.name: resid_lag
params.label: Information/perception lag before the pipeline reacts

params.name: fear
params.label: Applicant deterrence from visible AI progress (max fill-rate loss)
params.note: DR PGY-1 applicants fell 14% over 2023-2026 even as positions hit records and still filled 97.6%. In a 32-school survey, radiology's first-choice share fell from 21.4% to 17.7% when students considered AI.

params.name: fte_drift
params.label: Drift in FTE per radiologist (part-time, generational preferences)

params.name: adj_speed
params.label: Market adjustment speed: share of the remaining shortage or surplus closed each year
params.note: A truncated normal matching the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of the history test's fit to the documented job market of 1995-2013 (0.20, 0.40, 0.55, under a 0-0.6 prior). History disfavours slow adjustment (below about 0.2 per year) but with a wider prior allows up to about 0.7, so the cut at 0.6 is a judgment. With it, the held-out 2015-2025 episodes are predicted far better than without. The radiology job market has repeatedly self-corrected within a few years, faster than the training pipeline allows: work moved to non-radiologists while radiologists were scarce (their imaging grew twice as fast in 1998-2005), and radiologists' output per FTE rose 70% in 1992-2007 as PACS and teleradiology spread. The reverse flows during surpluses are assumed, not observed directly.

params.name: adj_max
params.label: Largest cumulative market adjustment (share of radiologist work that can shift)
params.note: A truncated normal matching the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of the history test's fit to 1995-2013 (0.08, 0.19, 0.28, under a 0-0.3 prior). History disfavours a weak adjustment (about 10% of the weight below 0.08, against a prior share of 27%) but cannot bound it from above, because past imbalances never exceeded about 10-15%; the cut at 0.3 is a judgment. Beyond the limit, imbalances are not absorbed: AI-driven changes larger than the historical swings still show up as shortage or surplus.

main.label: This site's assumptions
main.note: Imaging growth per person starts near 1.2%/yr.

ai_skeptic.label: AI-skeptical
ai_skeptic.note: Stall/Trend/Fast/Transformative weights 30/55/12/3%, nearer forecasting panels, which put far lower odds on transformative AI than AI-lab leaders.

ai_bullish.label: AI-bullish
ai_bullish.note: Stall/Trend/Fast/Transformative weights 5/35/30/30%, nearer AI-lab leaders and AI 2027 (a widely read scenario of very fast AI progress).

imaging_restraint.label: Imaging restraint
imaging_restraint.note: Imaging per person grows ~0.4%/yr: close to claims-based 2018-22 trends, plus payer and Medicare cost pressure (v1.5 assumed 0.6%/yr).

imaging_growth.label: Imaging growth
imaging_growth.note: Imaging per person grows ~1.8%/yr: what the history reconstruction implies for 2022-2026, near recent CT growth.

residency_slows.label: Residency growth slows
residency_slows.note: Positions grow only ~0.5%/yr as Medicare GME caps bind.

residency_growth.label: Residency growth continues
residency_growth.note: Residency positions keep growing ~1.9%/yr, the 2010-2025 pace.

favorable.label: Lowest-risk combination: AI-skeptical + imaging growth
favorable.note: Combines the two single changes that lower oversupply risk most.

unfavorable.label: Highest-risk combination: AI-bullish + imaging restraint
unfavorable.note: Combines the two single changes that raise oversupply risk most.

no_signoff.label: No radiologist on AI-first reads
no_signoff.detail: No audit or sign-off time at all on AI-first reads

unordered.label: Tiers automated in any order
unordered.detail: Complex exams may be automated before simple ones

open_demand.label: Much more new imaging
open_demand.detail: 3× as many new AI-enabled imaging uses and 2× the new radiologist tasks

payer_pushback.label: Stronger payer pushback
payer_pushback.detail: Payers' AI blocks twice as many scans; twice as many reads shift to other doctors

uncapped_new_uses.label: New uses not capped by scanners
uncapped_new_uses.detail: New uses such as screening existing scans are not limited by scanner capacity

tai_gated.label: Transformative boost waits for regulation
tai_gated.detail: Transformative AI's extra time savings must also wait for regulation and adoption

no_adjustment.label: No market adjustment (other v1.6 inputs kept)
no_adjustment.detail: Market adjustment removed (v1.5's design) but v1.6's other inputs kept; those were calibrated with the adjustment on

shortage_only.label: Surpluses not absorbed
shortage_only.detail: The market absorbs shortages as fitted but not surpluses: work does not flow back to radiologists

adj_cap15.label: Adjustment limit at most 15%
adj_cap15.detail: Adjustment limit capped at 15% of demand, the largest gap seen in 1995-2026

adj_wide.label: Larger adjustment (limit up to 50%)
adj_wide.detail: Adjustment speed and limit as in the fit with wider priors (limit up to 50% of demand)

adj_start.label: Adjustment starts from its reconstructed 2026 state
adj_start.detail: The adjustment starts from the reconstruction's 2026 state instead of zero (less room to absorb a surplus if work already moved to radiologists)

assistive_only.label: Assistive AI only
assistive_only.detail: AI helps radiologists read but never reads first

no_ai.label: No further radiology AI
no_ai.detail: Radiology AI frozen at its 2026 level (other diagnostics such as AI-ECG still displace some imaging)

tier1_2022.label: Normal-X-ray AI capable since 2022
tier1_2022.detail: Tier-1 capability centred on 2022 (EU approval) instead of 2025. If AI could do this since 2022 and the FDA still has not approved it, regulation must be slow, so fewer fast-AI futures fit the facts

no_shortage_today.label: Little or no shortage today
no_shortage_today.detail: Today's supply ÷ demand anywhere from 0.95 to 1.03 (main model: full range 0.88-0.99)
